question: Assume today is 2026-08-23. You know nothing published after this date. Estimate the number of live births in South Korea in July 2026, as it will be first reported in the national statistics agency's monthly Population Trends release.

target.what: Number of live births occurring in South Korea during July 2026, as first published in Statistics Korea's monthly Population Trends (인구동향) release
target.publisher: Statistics Korea (KOSTAT), monthly Population Trends / 인구동향
target.cadence: monthly, typically released around the 4th week of the following month (so July 2026 data would first appear around late August 2026)
target.caveats: Counts births by month of occurrence (occurrence-based), registered via resident registration; provisional figures are subject to later revision. Working interpretation: national total, all live births, month of occurrence July 2026. Alternative: registration-based counts could differ slightly. Targ

candidates.hypothesis: July 2026 births follow the recent monthly level and seasonal pattern of July births; the most recent published months (through ~May/June 2026) anchor the level and July seasonal factor adjusts it.
candidates.data_to_find: Monthly live births for South Korea for each month 2023-2026 published before cutoff, especially July values for 2023, 2024, 2025 and the latest months (Jan-Jun 2026) if released; month-on-month and year-on-year ratios for July.

candidates.hypothesis: Monthly resident-registration birth counts (행정안전부 주민등록 인구통계) track KOSTAT occurrence-based births closely and can proxy July 2026 before the official release.
candidates.data_to_find: Monthly resident registration births by month for 2024-2026, especially July 2026 if available, and the historical ratio of KOSTAT births to registration births.

candidates.hypothesis: Sum of regional monthly birth counts (시도별 출생) equals the national total; regional releases may appear earlier or provide partial July 2026 coverage.
candidates.data_to_find: Provincial monthly live birth counts for July 2026 or latest months, and the historical share of each province in the national total.

candidates.hypothesis: Births in a month ≈ women of childbearing age × age-specific fertility rates × days; or births ≈ births 9 months earlier conception proxies. Use annual births and monthly seasonal shares to derive July.
candidates.data_to_find: Annual 2025 births, 2026 year-to-date births, monthly seasonal distribution of births (share of July), and any fertility-rate or population-by-age data needed.

candidates.hypothesis: KOSTAT or media may publish projections or nowcasts of 2026 monthly births; these constrain the plausible range.
candidates.data_to_find: Any KOSTAT population projections, monthly birth nowcasts, or news reports citing expected July 2026 births published before cutoff.

candidates.hypothesis: Policy incentives (baby bonuses), marriage trends, and calendar effects (lunar holidays, weekends) shift monthly births; identify measurable exposure for July 2026.
candidates.data_to_find: Marriage registrations 2024-2026 (leading indicator ~9-12 months), birth incentive policy changes, and any known disruptions affecting July 2026 births.

previous_methods.rationale: Independent route: converts the strong Jan-May 2026 cumulative (p75) to a monthly average by dividing by the five-month window (a4, a fixed calendar constant) and applies a July seasonal factor. Does not rely on the single July 2025 base, so it hedges against a base-year anomaly. Failure mode: if the 2026 surge is concentrated in early months and fades by July, this route overstates; the seasonal factor band reflects that uncertainty.

previous_assumptions.name: July 2026 YoY growth factor vs July 2025
previous_assumptions.rationale: Jan-May 2026 cumulative births are +15.2% YoY (p75/p77) and May alone +13.6% (p17/p18); July 2025 was already a strong month (+5.9%, p109), so the YoY factor for July 2026 should be somewhat below the recent run-rate. Centered near 1.12 with a wide band reflecting possible fading of the surge.
previous_assumptions.applies_when: The recent double-digit YoY birth growth persists into July 2026, possibly moderating because July 2025 was a high base.
previous_assumptions.falsified_by: Evidence that June/July 2026 YoY growth collapsed toward zero or turned negative, or that July 2025 base was revised materially.

previous_assumptions.name: July seasonal factor relative to Jan-May 2026 monthly average
previous_assumptions.rationale: July births in Korea are typically slightly below the Jan-May average (July 2025 21,803 vs a 2025 monthly average near 21,200; July 2021 22,364 and July 2023 19,085 bracket the seasonal position). A factor just under 1 with a modest band is consistent with recent July shares.
previous_assumptions.applies_when: The 2026 monthly pattern retains the usual Korean seasonal shape with July modestly below the Jan-May average.
previous_assumptions.falsified_by: Evidence that 2026 July births were unusually high or low relative to the Jan-May run-rate (e.g., a strong July registration surge).

methods.label: m1

p63.role: July 2025 national live births in South Korea (KOSTAT occurrence-based)

a1.role: YoY growth factor for July 2026 vs July 2025

methods.rationale: Anchors on the same-month prior-year KOSTAT level (p63) and applies a YoY factor grounded in the observed 2026 surge (p75/p77, p17/p18). Shared dependency: the YoY factor is inferred from Jan-May 2026 data, so if the surge fades the estimate is too high; July 2025 being a strong base is the main reason the factor is below the recent run-rate.

methods.label: m2

p75.role: Jan-May 2026 cumulative national live births (5 months)

a2.role: July seasonal factor relative to the Jan-May 2026 monthly average

methods.rationale: Independent route: converts the strong Jan-May 2026 cumulative (p75) to a monthly average by dividing by the five-month window (literal 5, a fixed calendar constant) and applies a July seasonal factor. Does not rely on the single July 2025 base, so it hedges against a base-year anomaly. Failure mode: if the 2026 surge is concentrated in early months and fades by July, this route overstates; the se
methods.error: formula: numeric constant 5 not allowed (only 1 and exponents); make it a named input. If the number only converts units (1000 g per kg, days per year), drop it and set the method's "unit" to the unit the formula then gives (e.g. 'g/day'); code converts it to 'person'

combination.weight_gate: off: inverse backtest-error weights need a bank-level gate (>= 30 scored questions with >= 2 backtested routes, hit rate >= 0.7; METHODS_ZH 4.1), which has not been run

m1.note: Monte Carlo width below the default, not used to narrow

interval.rule: one block, so the interval is that block's own width

kept.name: July 2026 YoY growth factor vs July 2025
kept.rationale: Jan-May 2026 cumulative births are +15.2% YoY (p75/p77) and May alone +13.6% (p17/p18); July 2025 was already a strong month (+5.9%, p109), so the July 2026 YoY factor should sit somewhat below the recent run-rate. Centered near 1.12 with a wide band reflecting possible fading of the surge.
kept.applies_when: The recent double-digit YoY birth growth persists into July 2026, possibly moderating because July 2025 was a high base.
kept.falsified_by: Evidence that June/July 2026 YoY growth collapsed toward zero or turned negative, or that the July 2025 base was revised materially.

kept.name: July seasonal factor relative to Jan-May 2026 monthly average
kept.rationale: July births in Korea are typically slightly below the Jan-May average (July 2025 21,803 vs a 2025 monthly average near 21,200; July 2021 22,364 and July 2023 19,085 bracket the seasonal position). A factor just under 1 with a modest band is consistent with recent July shares.
kept.applies_when: The 2026 monthly pattern retains the usual Korean seasonal shape with July modestly below the Jan-May average.
kept.falsified_by: Evidence that 2026 July births were unusually high or low relative to the Jan-May run-rate (e.g., a strong July registration surge).

by_construction: Only URLs leave the searcher (code regex); extractor, judge and final prompts never contain search result titles, snippets or the searcher's text. This holds by construction and is not measured.
residual_risks: The searcher sees post-cutoff search results and chooses which URLs are fetched, so page selection can be conditioned on the answer; only the URLs leave the searcher, and in backtests every fetched page is a snapshot dated <= as_of.
Live pages are used only when as_of is today; in backtests every page is an archived snapshot dated <= as_of.
The leak sentinel only catches registered official values in common formats, not paraphrased or derived numbers.
The model's own training data (knowledge cutoff unpublished) can include history before as_of; it cannot include the target if the target was published after the model's release.
Wayback snapshots are captured by a third party; a snapshot date <= as_of proves the content existed by then.
Assumption values are proposed by the judge model from its own knowledge, which can include the target's history before as_of; code checks their form, not where the number came from.

The magnitude gate (v2.15d) asks the model once, without retrieval, for a rough estimate; whether the evidence-based estimate is more than 2x above or below it can carry the model's memory of the target into one repair. The rough number itself never enters a computation or a prompt; the estimate before that repair is kept in judge_rounds[-1].magnitude_checks[0]. The gate is off in the own-history ablation.
